title: They Pulled It Off: The Color Purple (2023) is Vastly Better Than the 80's Version (LONG POST)

commenti.body:
Great writeup, thank you for sharing it! I also thought it was great. This is my first experience with the story, and I was worried about the display of trauma going in. And despite how horrible Mister is I agree that his portrayal left room for male audience members to identify with, to see parts of themselves in him. The music video aspect was very present and there was so much momentum in some of the scenes like Shug Avery's Coming to Town. Like you said, I was dazzled in an old hollywood musical way, unafraid to be big and fantastical.

One thing though is that I feel the romantic relationship between Celie and Shug was almost hidden. It's a major plot point for sure with her pastor father and all, but outside of Celie and Shug in bed together in that one scene (which could be interpreted as friendship by some) I felt like you could have come away from the movie not realizing it at all. Like Shug's family disowned her because she's a singer, not queer. And Celie is never shown to have any other romantic relationship in the movie, or even one with Shug again. It's likely a natural response to her trauma, but it felt like Celie wasn't given the opportunity to show any kind of sexuality.

>It's a major plot point for sure with her pastor father and all, but outside of Celie and Shug in bed together in that one scene (which could be interpreted as friendship by some) I felt like you could have come away from the movie not realizing it at all.

Did you miss that they were actually making out in the theater? That seemed pretty explicit to me. It could've gone further. The book is basically a thesis on the cons and pros of lesbianism. At the same time, I don't think a woman like Shug back then would have considered herself lesbian or bisexual. So I can buy that aspect of her identity not really coming up in regards to her parents. 

Also was Tamela Mann supposed to be her mom? I was confused by that. I also do wish it aged them more as the years rolled by because Shug is apparently old enough to have a career and sexual flings when Celie is 15. So she's maybe in her mid 20's. She should be visibly in her 60's by then and her father should either be like 90 or dead. That's another thing that bothered me.

It slipped my mind but I do remember the scene of them in the balcony now. I'm guessing they didn't want to alienate homophobes too much, but I do agree it could have gone further. As for Shug I had assumed while watching that her parents did disown her exclusively for being lesbian, but I see now that may not have been public knowledge at all.

Yeah the aging was definitely a bit odd. Shug and her dad barely look like they aged at all. I suppose it's difficult to make them look different ages considering Taraji P. Henson and Tamela Mann are only 4 years apart irl.

>As for Shug I had assumed while watching that her parents did disown her exclusively for being lesbian, but I see now that may not have been public knowledge at all.

I do think sometimes it's important to try and put ourselves in the mind of the time period in which a film takes place. Queer identity was barely a formalized thing in the states at that time. I can buy a woman like Shug not necessarily defining herself by her sexuality that way. 

>I suppose it's difficult to make them look different ages considering Taraji P. Henson and Tamela Mann are only 4 years apart irl.

I kinda wish they had either cast someone as Young Shug and then we transition into Older Shug or they just make Taraji look older as time goes by and they did kinda try. Tbf, she looks insanely young to be 53. I would've put Tamela in some old lady wigs and did some aging makeup on her and David Alan Grier.

>I do think sometimes it's important to try and put ourselves in the mind of the time period in which a film takes place. Queer identity was barely a formalized thing in the states at that time. I can buy a woman like Shug not necessarily defining herself by her sexuality that way.

Sorry, I think I mis-spoke. While watching I knew queer identity would not be defined in that way, and I wouldn't plaster modern ideals onto characters in period pieces. I agree Shug and Celie wouldn't have labelled themselves or their relationship in that way, and may not have let anyone else know about it. I had heard about the sapphic aspects of the story and assumed there would be more in the movie about it, but it seems to only come up in the middle of the movie.

Agree on the aging, they weren't super consistent about keeping the continuity intact.

The musical does explore it more. There's a plotline carried over from the book where Shug asks Celie if she can have one more fling with this young guy in her band. This is what leads to 'I'm Still Here'. Originally she starts off singing 'I don't need you to love me, I don't need you to love'. You actually hear that instrumental before she breaks into the verse in the film. I can imagine they cut this plot thread because both in the book and the stage version it does make Shug somewhat unlikeable.
